extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics educators, and researchers interested in the cognitive/psychological processes of mathematical discovery and learning
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-style analysis of different modes of mathematical thought (intuition vs logic, role of imagery and language, student understanding, and the psychology of discovery). Gives descriptive criteria for how mathematicians think, discover, and how one should teach/verify mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of internal language vs imagery in thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a thinker carries thoughts primarily in words (internal speech) or in images/other signs; words may serve as labels and can both help and mislead reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text discusses variability among individuals: some think largely in words (typographic-visual/verbal types), others in imagery or nonverbal signs. Words can be useful but may produce misunderstandings if one mistakes words for reasons (examples: Max Müller, Ribot, Locke). Evaluate how much verbalization vs imagery is used and be cautious about assuming verbalized thought equals reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between full consciousness and fringe-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Many mathematical deductions involve an unconscious or fringe-conscious process such that the subject may remember the result or the formal schema but not the conscious chain of reasoning that produced it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that mathematical thought often allows one to leave a proof aside and retain only its conclusion; after constructing a deduction one may recall its development without the reasoning having been fully present to consciousness. When evaluating a mathematician's account or one's own thought, note whether steps are present only in the fringe and consider how that affects reproducibility and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and enunciation of relay-results (lemmas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making parts of a deduction explicit as relay-results simplifies synthesis and is essential for utilizability and certitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relay-results (intermediate lemmas) should be enunciated to make arguments usable and to permit extension. The text notes that necessary synthesis is greatly simplified when parts of a deduction are replaced by corresponding relay-results; teaching often increases relay-results to aid beginners at the cost of hiding the synthetic thread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetizability of proofs (rigorous, formalizably arithmetizable arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: A modern mathematical proof should be arithmetizable — i.e., able to be recast in fully arithmetical (or formal) terms — otherwise it is not satisfactory for the contemporary mathematician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that proofs (example: Jordan's theorem) are not satisfactory unless fully arithmetizable; for rigor and to be acceptable to the mathematical community, one must ensure that intuitive or geometric arguments can be translated into arithmetical/formal form when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: What it means to 'understand' a mathematical demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding a proof is not merely checking the correctness of each syllogism; it is knowing why the steps link together — grasping the synthetic thread that generates the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Poincaré: many students want to know not only that the syllogisms are correct but why they are arranged in that order. Teaching that forces every link into conscious form (verifying, 'precising', adding relay-results) may produce clarity but can eliminate the synthesis that gives direction and insight. Evaluate understanding by whether the student/reader grasps the generative logic, not only verifies steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical trade-off: explicit formalization vs preserving synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: For beginners, presenting every part of an argument consciously and increasing relay-results yields rigor and clarity, but may destroy the synthetic thread that guides discovery and deeper understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends explicit, fully conscious presentation for novices to get a rigorous foundation; however, teachers should be aware this risks producing students who can verify steps without possessing the synthetic intuition that leads discovery. Balance explicitness and preservation of synthesis in instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-sense (unconscious) reasoning vs scientific (formal) reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Common-sense deductions rely on superficial/unconscious data (sometimes empirical) and may give right or wrong conclusions; scientific reasoning requires verification, precision, and formal methods for difficult questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: commonsense conclusions about tangents or Jordan's theorem may be misleading or require heavy formal proof. When assessing reasoning, do not accept commonsense in place of arithmetized/formal demonstration for nontrivial mathematical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth level of the unconscious where ideas combine
rubrics_metrics.description: The depth at which starting ideas ('atoms') meet and combine in the unconscious influences whether a mind appears more 'intuitive' (deeper layers) or more 'logical' (shallower layers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If idea-combination happens in deep unconscious layers, the discoverer may not be able to bring the path to full consciousness (examples: Hermite, Fermat). If combinations are closer to consciousness, the mind will more readily articulate the steps (example: Poincaré). Consider depth when judging ability to explain or teach discoveries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of scattering vs narrowness of idea projection
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the projection of initial ideas (Poincaré's 'atoms') is scattered or narrowly directed affects the character of thought: scattered projections tend to produce intuition-like leaps; narrowly directed thought tends to produce logical, stepwise development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is independent of the unconscious depth. Evaluate whether a mathematician's idea-space is broad (favoring unexpected syntheses) or narrowly focused (favoring methodical derivations) to understand their approach and to tailor evaluation or collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and role of auxiliary representations
rubrics_metrics.description: The type of auxiliary signs (geometrical images, auditory/musical imagery, verbal labels, personal ad hoc signs) used to sustain thought greatly affects the course of discovery and exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jakobson's distinction: social (conventional) signs vs personal signs, with personal signs further subdivided into constant (habitual) and episodical (ad hoc). Titchener trained varied imagery to avoid becoming overly verbal. When evaluating a solution or explanation, note which representations were used and whether they facilitate communication and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility and normality of 'paradoxical' intuitive discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Some discoveries are achieved by intuition where essential links are unknown to the discoverer; later, new mathematical frameworks (tools) are required to supply formal proofs (Fermat, Riemann examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that a convincing informal argument or asserted result may be historically or cognitively plausible even if the discoverer did not possess or record a full formal proof. Evaluation should distinguish between heuristic/intuitive discovery and availability of a later rigorous justification; both have scientific value but different statuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training of imagery (auto-education) to broaden mental representations
rubrics_metrics.description: One can deliberately cultivate a wider variety and richer imagery (visual, auditory, musical) to counter excessive verbal thinking and to enhance creative thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titchener's practice: he trained himself to use visual and auditory imagery to prevent becoming overly verbal with age. For practitioners and students, deliberate exercises to develop nonverbal imagery can be recommended as a means to preserve intuitive resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of mistaking words for reasons (linguistic misleading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language may disguise lack of genuine reasoning: clear words do not guarantee correct or deep thought; one can be 'deranged' by words into apparent understanding without true logical grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary references: Max Müller, Ribot, and others warn that words can look clear while thought is muddled. When assessing explanations, probe whether language is serving as a mere label or whether it reflects underlying justification.
